routes.description: Establish that universally binding moral truths require a nonhuman objective standard, identify that standard with God's immutable and revealed character, and show that secular welfare, preference, convention, and contract accounts cannot supply equivalent moral objectivity or obligation.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if objective moral absolutes are established, God's necessary character is shown to ground both their truth and authority, and the proposed secular standards are shown unable to explain their universality, nonarbitrariness, or prescriptive force.

motionBridge.description: Show that objective moral truth and obligation require God's character as their necessary, nonhuman foundation.

centralBridges.description: Establish that at least some actions possess universally true moral status independent of individual or collective preference.
Explain how God's immutable character, rather than an arbitrary divine choice, constitutes the objective moral standard.
Show why consequence, preference, convention, and contractual agreement cannot generate universally binding moral duties.
Connect God's nature, creative authority, and purposes to prescriptions that bind human agents.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how revelation and divine omniscience provide access to moral requirements and informed guidance about their application.
Use difficult cases to test whether harm-oriented secular standards preserve the moral judgments they purport to explain.

routes.description: Reject the claimed necessity of a divine foundation by distinguishing definitions from objectively assessable judgments, grounding moral inquiry in real consequences, intentions, and impartial rule construction, and showing that divine-nature claims do not independently explain goodness or obligation.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if a coherent secular method can yield objective assessments or justified rules without God, or if the divine account fails to establish moral absolutes, nonarbitrary goodness, or a valid transition from facts about God to binding duties.

motionBridge.description: Show that God is not required for defensible moral truth or obligation because secular inquiry is viable or divine grounding is explanatorily incomplete.

centralBridges.description: Distinguish the selection of a moral standard from the objective truth of judgments concerning suffering, consequences, intentions, and circumstances.
Explain how welfare-sensitive reasoning and impartial contractual construction can justify rules without presupposing divine existence.
Test whether identifying goodness with God's nature makes the divine standard circular, arbitrary, or modally unexplained.
Require an account of how descriptions of God's nature, power, creation, or judgment entail reasons or duties to obey.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish God's possible role as an omniscient source of information from the facts that make conduct morally right or wrong.
Separate the existence or justification of moral requirements from motivation, compliance, punishment, and practical deterrence.

sections.title: Moral Objectivity and the Existence of Absolutes
sections.rationale: Defines the phenomenon requiring explanation and tests whether morality involves intrinsic universal truths, objectively assessable claims under a chosen standard, or context-sensitive judgments about consequences and intentions.

sections.title: Divine Nature, Necessity, and Nonarbitrariness
sections.rationale: Addresses whether God's immutable character supplies a necessary moral standard or leaves unresolved circularity, contrary-nature possibilities, and the basis for calling the divine character good.

sections.title: Secular Welfare and Impartial Rule Construction
sections.rationale: Examines whether facts about suffering, potential conscious states, social consequences, and veil-of-ignorance reasoning can support objective assessments or justified rules without God.

sections.title: Moral Obligation and the Is-Ought Bridge
sections.rationale: Tests how either foundation produces binding prescriptions, with particular attention to whether creation, ownership, divine purposes, definitions, or secular commitments provide reasons agents ought to act.

sections.title: Omniscience, Revelation, and Moral Knowledge
sections.rationale: Distinguishes the metaphysical ground of morality from access to relevant facts and evaluates whether omniscience and revelation establish foundation, reliable guidance, or only informational authority.

sections.title: Counterexamples, Motivation, and Practical Force
sections.rationale: Organizes the disputed cases involving hidden harm, rule consequences, disobedience, punishment, and deterrence to test each account without conflating moral truth with motivation or compliance.

chunk-001:c001.proposition: Moral truth requires a mind-grounded, nonarbitrary source, while an atheistic appeal to consequences cannot impose universally binding moral values.

chunk-001:c003.proposition: Morality is grounded in God's immutable nature and essence rather than arbitrary commands, and that enduring standard is disclosed through divine self-revelation.

chunk-001:c006.proposition: A hypothetical that reverses God's essential holy and righteous character cannot test divine morality because it replaces the theological subject whose nature grounds the standard.

chunk-001:c009.proposition: God knows all actual and potential facts, so divine moral revelations may rest on relevant reasons that limited human agents cannot fully understand.

chunk-002:c002-01.proposition: Because God knows every end result, divine omniscience permits perfect moral judgments and informed prescriptions about which actions agents should and should not perform.

chunk-002:c002-05.proposition: Given moral absolutes that require an objective standard, the failure of atheistic systems to justify such a standard leaves the theistic account validated by impossibility to the contrary.

chunk-002:c002-06.proposition: Torturing babies to death merely for pleasure is wrong for everyone, and God's revealed prohibition on murder supplies the standard supporting that universal judgment.

chunk-002:c002-08.proposition: A secret assault on an unconscious person remains wrong even when awareness, pregnancy, disease, discovery, and other stipulated harms are absent, challenging a harm-only moral criterion.

chunk-003:chunk-003-candidate-01.proposition: A recipient-preference account can assign opposite moral statuses to the same conduct depending on what a recipient wants and therefore cannot furnish an objective standard.

chunk-003:chunk-003-candidate-07.proposition: A Christian may knowingly violate acknowledged moral requirements, but inconsistency between profession and practice does not undermine the existence of objective moral truth.

chunk-004:chunk-004-candidate-02.proposition: Christianity can bridge the is-ought gap because its account includes prescriptions, whereas an arbitrary atheistic system cannot derive a binding ought from descriptions alone.

chunk-004:chunk-004-candidate-04.proposition: People ought to do what is right because right conduct is consistent with and glorifies God, the supreme object of worship and the proper moral standard.

chunk-001:c002.proposition: Secular moral inquiry can adopt the substantive aim of promoting flourishing and reducing unnecessary suffering while recognizing that the definition of morality is not itself a truth claim.

chunk-001:c005.proposition: God's fixed identity does not explain why an eternally contrary divine nature is impossible, leaving the alleged necessity and nonarbitrariness of the divine moral standard unexplained.

chunk-001:c007.proposition: If God is the sole standard by which God is evaluated, believers lack a noncircular basis for determining that the divine standard is good rather than profoundly harmful.

chunk-001:c008.proposition: A divine-nature account supplies no rational reason to obey God when its justification that God is good reduces to the circular claim that God conforms to God's own nature.

chunk-002:c002-02.proposition: If consequences determine which actions are right, omniscience makes God an informational intermediary who communicates those facts rather than the foundation that makes the actions right.

chunk-002:c002-04.proposition: As with conventional measurement standards, a moral definition may be selected by humans while particular judgments assessed against that standard remain objectively true or false.

chunk-002:c002-09.proposition: Secular moral reasoning can evaluate actual and potential conscious states together with rule-level social consequences rather than merely maximizing immediate aggregate happiness.

chunk-002:c002-10.proposition: Hypothetical rational construction behind a veil of ignorance can generate impartial rules for social conduct without presupposing the existence or authority of God.

chunk-003:chunk-003-candidate-04.proposition: A divine moral theory can separate right and wrong entirely from suffering, happiness, and health because a divine nature favoring universal misery would make misery moral by definition.

chunk-003:chunk-003-candidate-06.proposition: Even accepting Christianity's factual and moral claims does not by itself supply a motivating reason that compels an agent to obey the divine prescriptions the agent believes are true.

chunk-004:chunk-004-candidate-03.proposition: Facts that God created humanity, is powerful, defines morality, or can punish people remain descriptions that do not by themselves explain why anyone ought to obey God.
